sections.title: Introduction to the Department
sections.text:
The idea of the Mechatronics Engineering Department at the Federal University of Technology (FUT), Minna was conceived in 2010 as one of the departments in the School of Engineering and Engineering Technology, alongside Telecommunication, Computer, Mechanical, Civil, Electrical and Electronics, Agricultural and Bio-Resources, and Chemical Engineering. The Department was officially granted take-off approval during the 2014/2015 academic session after passing through a series of accreditations by the Nigerian Universities Commission, and admitted its first set of students in the 2015/2016 academic session.

Mechatronics refers to the efficient and effective integration of mechanical systems and electronics. It is a blend of mechanics and electronics, and has come to mean the synergistic use of precision engineering, control theory, computer science, mathematics and sensor technology to design enhanced or "smart" products, processes and systems. As an academic discipline it combines elements of electrical engineering, computer engineering, telecommunication engineering, control engineering, materials engineering, mechanical engineering and computer science.

sections.title: Philosophy of the Programme
sections.text:
The philosophy establishing Universities of Technology in Nigeria is to build national capacity to move the country from its present status of a third-world developing nation to that of an advanced and developed nation, through technological advancement that drives development and develops high-level manpower that will create jobs and wealth.

Mechatronics Engineering is one of the most dynamic areas of engineering in recent times. The general philosophy of the department hinges on the development of competencies in core mechatronics subject areas capable of contributing to national goals and aspirations through pragmatic, self-reliant and socio-economic driven technological advancement. The core areas include: Mechatronics System Development; Artificial Intelligence Systems; Machine Vision and Image Processing; Robotics and Automation; Control and Instrumentation; Autotronics; Electronics and Embedded Systems; Digital Signal Processing; and Computer System Engineering.

sections.title: Vision of the Department
sections.text: The vision of the department is to be a world-class Centre of Excellence in Mechatronics Engineering, graduating world-class students of high academic standard, with adequate practical skills and exposure capable of enabling them to fit into either an academic or an industrial set-up.

sections.title: Mission of the Department
sections.text: The department will harness all available human and material resources in providing high-quality mechatronics engineering goods and services for the Nigerian community through quality training of students, qualitative research and entrepreneurship skills for a self-reliant and self-sustaining economy.

sections.title: Objectives of the Programme
sections.text: The objectives of the B.Eng. Programme in Mechatronics Engineering are: (a) to produce graduates with competencies in Mechatronics Engineering design and analysis; (b) to provide research opportunities in Mechatronics Engineering or related disciplines; (c) to provide required advanced professional knowledge in the industrial set-up; (d) to establish linkages and collaboration with related industries in providing training, skills and equipment for process automation and mechanization; and (e) to produce engineers that are capable of engaging in entrepreneurial activities that apply Mechatronics Engineering knowledge and technical skills.

sections.title: Areas of Specialization
sections.text: The areas of specialization in the Mechatronics Engineering Department are: (i) Mechatronics System Development; (ii) Artificial Intelligence Systems; (iii) Electronics and Embedded Systems; (iv) Robotics and Automation; (v) Digital Signal Processing; (vi) Machine Vision and Image Processing; (vii) Control and Instrumentation; (viii) Autotronics; (ix) Precision Agriculture; (x) Internet of Things; and (xi) Computer System Engineering.

sections.title: Competencies of the Graduates
sections.text:
The rapid pace of change in the computing field requires Mechatronics engineers to be life-long learners so as to maintain their knowledge and skills within their chosen area of specialization. Mechatronics engineers generally should satisfy three characteristics: (a) possess the ability to design complex systems that include both hardware and software needed for solving novel engineering problems, subject to trade-offs involving competing goals and constraints — here "design" refers to a level of ability beyond "assembling" or "configuring" systems; (b) have a breadth of knowledge in mathematics and engineering sciences beyond that narrowly required for the field; and (c) acquire and maintain a preparation for professional practice in engineering.

The programme develops graduates in competence and skills including: analysing data in alternative forms to create deeper understanding; use of relevant test and measurement equipment, including assembling and using experimental laboratory and workshop set-ups, and estimating errors and accuracy of measurements; researching for information to develop ideas further and working with limited or contradictory information; use of information technology tools, including programming languages and a broad understanding of common information tools; applying engineering techniques taking industrial and commercial constraints into account, learning independently and understanding new concepts; and competence in teamwork and leadership.

sections.title: Job Opportunities for Graduates
sections.text: Students graduating from the department shall be strongly equipped to seek careers at: (a) robotics and manufacturing companies; (b) automobile and autotronics industries; (c) computer manufacturing companies; (d) telecommunications companies; (e) oil and gas companies; (f) research institutes; (g) teaching and lecturing in schools, colleges and universities; and (h) any 21st-century ICT-driven company.

sections.title: UTME Admission Requirements
sections.text:
There are two modes of admission into the Bachelor Degree Mechatronics Engineering Programme at FUT Minna: the UTME mode and the Direct Entry (DE) mode.

For UTME admission a candidate needs: (a) credit in five O'Level subjects at GCE, SSCE or an equivalent, which must include Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, English Language and any other science subject such as Biology, Agricultural Science or Further Mathematics — the five credits must be obtained at not more than two sittings; and (b) candidates are required to sit for and pass the University Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME) in English Language, Mathematics, Chemistry and Physics.

sections.title: Direct Entry Admission Requirements
sections.text: For Direct Entry admission: (a) holders of Upper Credit level in a National Diploma (ND) in Electrical, Computer, Mechatronics or Mechanical Engineering may qualify for admission at 200 Level, in addition to the O'Level requirements; (b) GCE A'Level or IJMB with credit passes in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry may also qualify for 200 Level; (c) holders of an HND with at least Upper Credit in Electrical, Electronic, Computer, Mechatronics or Mechanical Engineering, plus the O'Level requirements, may qualify for admission at 300 Level, while holders of HSC/GCE A'Level/IJMBE with credit passes in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry may qualify for 200 Level; and (d) Direct Entry candidates are required to hold the O'Level grades stipulated in the UTME requirements, and must also take and pass the General Studies (GST) courses offered at 100 and 200 Levels.

sections.title: Programme Structure and Student Evaluation
sections.text:
The programme workload combines conventional formal university lectures, tutorials, practical sessions, laboratory work, seminars and a project. Periodically at 200, 300, 400 and 500 Levels, Mechatronics Engineering students go on excursions to industries that deploy mechatronics, automation and ICT in their operations, for industrial experience. At 500 Level, students carry out an independent project in their area of specialization.

Students are evaluated through: (a) Continuous Assessment, made up of assignments and tests, forming 40% of the evaluation; and (b) Examination, making up 60% of the total evaluation. To qualify for a course examination, a student is required to achieve 75% attendance of all the scheduled classes for the course.

sections.title: Duration of the Programme
sections.text:
The Bachelor of Engineering Programme in Mechatronics Engineering is normally a five-year programme (100–500 Levels). Direct Entry candidates normally spend four years (A'Level and OND candidates) or three years (HND candidates). The programme is structured so that all engineering students offer the same basic courses at 100 and 200 Levels to prepare them for the profession; the 300 to 500 Level courses are more detailed and focused on training in Mechatronics Engineering.

A student cannot stay beyond one hundred and fifty percent (150%) of the normal duration of the programme, i.e. 7.5, 6 and 4.5 sessions for the 5, 4 and 3-year programmes respectively. In semesters: UTME entry takes a minimum of 10 and a maximum of 15 semesters; 200 Level Direct Entry takes a minimum of 8 and a maximum of 12 semesters.

sections.title: Graduation Requirements
sections.text:
To graduate, a student must be found worthy in character throughout the period of studentship in the university and must accumulate the total units prescribed by the School from core courses, electives, General Studies courses, SWEP/SIWES and the final-year project.

For UTME entry the unit breakdown is: Basic Sciences 37, Major Engineering 129, Electives 8, Social Science 6, General Studies 10, SIWES 6, SWEP 2 — a total of 198 units. For 200 Level Direct Entry: Major Engineering 125, Electives 8, Social Science 6, General Studies 5, SIWES 6, SWEP 2 — a total of 152 units.

sections.title: 100 Level Course Structure
sections.text:
100 Level First Semester (20 units): MAT111 Elementary Mathematics I — Algebra and Trigonometry (3); MAT112 Elementary Mathematics III — Vectors, Geometry and Dynamics (3); GST110 Use of English I and Library (3); PHY113 General Physics I — Mechanics, Thermal Physics and Waves (3); CHM111 General Chemistry I (3); CPT111 Introduction to Computer Science (3); STA117 Descriptive Statistics (2).

100 Level Second Semester (23 units): MAT121 Elementary Mathematics II — Calculus (3); CPT121 Introduction to Problem Solving (3); GST103 Nigerian Peoples and Culture (2); GST121 Use of English II (2); PHY100 General Physics Laboratory (2); PHY123 General Physics II — Electricity, Magnetism and Modern Physics (3); PHY126 General Physics III (2); CHM121 General Chemistry II (3); CHM191 Practical Chemistry (2); EET121 History and Philosophy of Science (1).

sections.title: 200 Level Course Structure
sections.text:
200 Level First Semester (22 units): EET211 Engineering Mathematics I (3); EET212 Applied Mechanics (3); EET213 Engineering Drawing I (2); EET214 Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics (2); EET215 Strength of Materials I (2); EET216 Materials Science (2); EET217 General Engineering Laboratory I (3); EET218 Engineer-in-the-Society (1); EET219 Basic Electrical Engineering I (2); GST208 Entrepreneurship 1 (2).

200 Level Second Semester (23 units): MCE220 Fundamentals of Mechatronics (1); EET221 Engineering Mathematics II (3); EET222 Engineering Thermodynamics I (2); EET223 Engineering Drawing II (2); EET224 General Computer Programming (3); EET225 Workshop Practice (2); EET226 Information Technology in Engineering (2); EET227 General Engineering Laboratory II (3); EET229 Basic Electrical Engineering II (2); ELE221 Basic Electronics (3).

At the end of the Second Semester of 200 Level, students take the Students Work Experience Programme (SWEP), worth 2 units.

sections.title: 300 Level Course Structure
sections.text:
300 Level First Semester (23 units): ELE311 Applied Mathematics for Electrical Engineers I (3, pre-requisite EET211); ELE312 Measurement and Instrumentation (3); ELE313 Signals and Systems (2); ELE314 Circuit Theory (3); ELE315 Analogue Electronic Circuits (3, pre-requisite ELE221); ELE316 General Electrical Laboratory Practical (3); MCE311 Control Engineering I (2); CPE311 Computer Programming and Languages (2); GST308 Entrepreneurship II (2).

300 Level Second Semester (23 units): ELE321 Applied Mathematics for Electrical Engineers II (3, pre-requisite EET221); ELE322 Field Theory (3); ELE323 Principles of Electromechanical Conversion (2); ELE324 Digital Electronic Circuit (3, pre-requisite ELE221); MCE321 Sensors and Actuators (3); MCE322 Control Engineering II (2); MCE323 Introduction to Robotics (3); MCE324 Computer Software Engineering (2); MCE325 Mechatronics Systems Laboratory I (2).

At the end of the Second Semester of 300 Level, students take the Student Industrial Work Experience Scheme I (SIWES I), worth 2 units.

sections.title: 400 Level Course Structure
sections.text:
400 Level First Semester (18 units): ELE411 Research Methods and Communications (2); MCE411 Fluid Power Systems II (2, pre-requisite EET214); MCE412 Computer Aided Design and Manufacturing (2); MCE413 Mechatronics Systems Design (3); MCE414 MEMS and VLSI (2); MCE415 Digital Image Processing Systems and Application (3); MCE416 Mechatronics Systems Laboratory II (2); MCE400 Mechatronics Capstone Project (2).

400 Level Second Semester: SIW400 SIWES II (6 units). The whole second semester of 400 Level is spent on the Student Industrial Work Experience Scheme II in industry.

sections.title: 500 Level Course Structure
sections.text:
500 Level First Semester (18 units): ELE511 Management and Law for Electrical Engineers (2); ELE512 Digital Signal Processing (2); EEE514 Power Electronics and Drives (2); CPE510 Artificial Intelligence and Applications (2); MCE511 Robotics and Automation (2, pre-requisite MCE323); MCE512 Vibrations (2); MCE513 Digital Systems and PLC (2) — sub-total 14 units. Electives (4 units required from): MCE531 Machine Vision (2); MCE532 Modern Control (2, pre-requisite MCE311); EEE518 Energy Studies (2); CPE519 Internet of Things (2).

500 Level Second Semester (18 units): ELE521 Reliability Methods in Electrical Engineering and Technology (2); MCE521 Microcontrollers and Embedded Systems (2, pre-requisite MCE413); MCE522 Process Control and Automation (2, pre-requisite MCE322); MCE523 Systems Modelling and Simulation (2); MCE599 Final Year Project (6) — sub-total 14 units. Electives (4 units required from): MCE541 Intelligent Control Systems (2, pre-requisite MCE322); MCE542 Digital Signal Processor-Based Systems (2); MCE543 Autonomous and Mobile Robotic Systems (2, pre-requisite MCE323).

sections.title: Course Descriptions — 100 Level First Semester
sections.text:
MAT111 Elementary Mathematics I — Algebra and Trigonometry (3 units): Elementary set theory, subsets, union, intersection, complements, Venn diagrams. Real numbers; integers, rational and irrational numbers, mathematical induction, real sequences and series, theory of quadratic equations, binomial theorem. Complex numbers; algebra of complex numbers; the Argand diagram; De Moivre's theorem; nth roots of unity. Circular measure, trigonometric functions of angles of any magnitude, addition and factor formulae.

MAT112 Elementary Mathematics III — Vectors, Geometry and Dynamics (3 units): Geometric representation of vectors in 1–3 dimensions, components, direction cosines. Addition and scalar multiplication of vectors, linear independence. Scalar and vector products of two vectors. Differentiation and integration of vectors with respect to a scalar variable. Two-dimensional coordinate geometry: straight lines, circles, parabola, ellipse, hyperbola, tangents and normals. Impact of two smooth spheres and of a sphere on a smooth surface.

GST110 Use of English I and Library (3 units): Communication and the elements of the communication process; effective essay writing; academic sources of information; answering examination questions; technical report writing, including the definition, purpose, attributes, categories and structure of technical reports, and research report writing. The Use of Library part covers the nature and concept of the library, the five fundamental laws of librarianship and types of libraries.

PHY113 General Physics I — Mechanics, Thermal Physics and Waves (3 units): Space and time, units and dimensions, kinematics; fundamental laws of mechanics, statics and dynamics; work and energy; conservation laws. Elasticity; Hooke's law; Young's, shear and bulk moduli. Hydrostatics; pressure; buoyancy; Archimedes' principle; surface tension; adhesion, cohesion, capillarity, drops and bubbles. Temperature; heat; gas laws; laws of thermodynamics; kinetic theory of gases; sound; applications.

CHM111 General Chemistry I (3 units): Atoms, molecules and chemical reactions. Modern electronic theory of atoms. Electronic configuration, periodicity and the periodic table. Hybridization and shapes of simple molecules. Valence forces; structure of solids. Chemical equations and stoichiometry; chemical bonding and intermolecular forces; kinetic theory of matter. Elementary thermochemistry; rates of reaction, equilibrium and thermodynamics. Acids, bases and salts. Properties of gases. Redox reactions and introduction to electrochemistry. Radioactivity.

CPT111 Introduction to Computer Science: History of computers, functional components of a computer, characteristics of a computer, problem solving, flowcharts, algorithms, computer programming, statements, symbolic names, arrays, subscripts, expressions and control statements, introduction to the FORTRAN programming language, computer applications.

STA117 Descriptive Statistics (2 units): Statistical data — types, sources and methods of collection. Presentation of data: tables, charts and graphs. Errors and approximations. Frequency and cumulative distributions. Measures of location, partition, dispersion, skewness and kurtosis. Rates, ratios and index numbers.

sections.title: Course Descriptions — 100 Level Second Semester
sections.text:
MAT121 Elementary Mathematics II — Calculus (3 units): Vector and scalar field functions, complex numbers, linear algebra, basis, rank and nullity, determinants; functions of variables, graphs, limits and the idea of continuity; the derivative as a limit of change; techniques of differentiation; extrema and curve sketching; integration as the inverse of differentiation; methods of integration; definite integrals; application to areas and volumes.

CPT121 Introduction to Problem Solving (3 units): Brief survey of programming paradigms — procedural, object-oriented and functional. Introduction to Visual Basic (VB): history and versions. Fundamental programming constructs in VB: syntax and semantics; variables, types, expressions and assignment; simple input/output; conditional and iterative control structures; testing and debugging strategies.

GST103 Nigerian Peoples and Culture (2 units): A survey of Nigerian peoples and culture, covering Nigerian history, culture and arts in pre-colonial times; the evolution of Nigeria as a political unit; the indigene/settler phenomenon; concepts of trade; economic self-reliance; social justice and individual and national development; norms and values; reorientation of moral and national values; and moral obligations of citizens.

GST121 Use of English II — Reading, Composition and Oral (2 units): Reading techniques and study skills; reading purposes and strategies; skimming, scanning and SQ3R; identifying main ideas; summary writing; vocabulary development, registers and lexis, American and British vocabulary differences; oral skills — listening comprehension, speaking, the English sound system (vowels, consonants and diphthongs), the art of public speaking; literary terms and poetic devices.

PHY100 General Physics Laboratory I (2 units): Laboratory experiments covering the main aspects of PHY113, PHY123 and PHY126, after an introduction to quantitative measurement techniques, the treatment of errors and graphical analysis.

PHY123 General Physics II — Electricity, Magnetism and Modern Physics (3 units): Electric field and electric potential; electric charge; electrostatics; Coulomb's law; Gauss's theorem; equipotentials; capacitance; parallel-plate and practical capacitors, capacitors in series and parallel, stored energy, dielectrics, charging and discharging a capacitor. Magnetic fields and induction; Maxwell's equations; electromagnetic oscillations and waves; applications.

PHY126 General Physics III (2 units): Molecular treatment of the properties of matter; elasticity; Hooke's law; Young's, shear and bulk moduli. Hydrostatics; pressure; buoyancy; Archimedes' principle. Hydrodynamics; streamlines; Bernoulli and continuity equations; turbulence; Reynolds number; viscosity; laminar flow; Poiseuille's equation. Surface tension; adhesion, cohesion, capillarity, drops and bubbles. Temperature; the zeroth law of thermodynamics; heat; gas laws; laws of thermodynamics; kinetic theory of gases; applications.

CHM121 General Chemistry II (3 units): Historical survey of the development and importance of organic chemistry; fullerenes as the fourth allotrope of carbon, nanotubes, nanostructures and nanochemistry. Electronic theory in organic chemistry. Isolation and purification of organic compounds. Determination of the structures of organic compounds, including qualitative and quantitative analysis. Nomenclature and functional-group classes of organic compounds. Introductory reaction mechanisms and kinetics. Stereochemistry. The chemistry of alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, alcohols, ethers, amines, alkyl halides, nitriles, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and derivatives. Chemistry of selected metals and non-metals; comparative chemistry of Group IA, IIA and IVA elements; introduction to transition-metal chemistry.

CHM191 General Chemistry Practical I (2 units): Laboratory experiments designed to reflect the topics in CHM111 and CHM121, including acid–base titrations, qualitative analysis, redox reactions, gravimetric analysis, data analysis and presentation.

EET121 History and Philosophy of Science (1 unit): Man — his origin and nature; man and his cosmic environment; scientific methodology; science and technology in the society and service of man; renewable and non-renewable resources; environmental effects of chemicals, plastics, textiles and wastes; chemical and radiochemical hazards; introduction to the various areas of science and technology; elements of environmental studies.

sections.title: Course Descriptions — 200 Level First Semester
sections.text:
EET211 Engineering Mathematics I (3 units): Complex analysis — elements of complex algebra, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions. Real numbers, sequences and series. Vectors — elements, differentiation and integration. Elements of linear algebra.

EET212 Applied Mechanics (3 units): Statics — laws of statics, systems of forces and their properties; friction. Particle dynamics — kinematics of plane motion; Newton's laws; kinetics of particles; momentum and energy methods. Kinematics of rigid bodies — velocity and acceleration diagrams. Kinetics of rigid bodies — two-dimensional motion, energy and momentum; mass moment of inertia; simple harmonic motion.

EET213 Engineering Drawing I (2 units): Use of drafting instruments, lettering, dimensioning and drawing layout. Engineering graphics — geometrical figures and conics. Graphical calculus and applications. Development and intersection of curves and solids. Projections — lines, planes and simple solids; orthographic and isometric projections. Threaded fasteners. Pictorial and freehand sketching. Conventional practices.

EET214 Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics (2 units): Elements of fluid statics — density, pressure, surface tension, viscosity, compressibility, capillarity, solubility. Fluid statics — flotation and stability; hydrostatic forces on submerged surfaces due to incompressible fluids. Introduction to fluid dynamics and conservation laws. Introduction to viscous flow. Dimensional analysis and dynamic similitude.

EET215 Strength of Materials I (2 units): Force equilibrium and free-body diagrams. Concepts of stress and strain; the tensile test; Young's moduli and other strength factors. Axially loaded bars, composite bars, temperature stresses and simple indeterminate problems. Hoop stress; cylinders and rings. Bending moment, shear force and axial force diagrams for simple cases. Properties of sections (centroids and moments of areas). Introduction to deflection (double integration and Macaulay's method). Simple torsion and applications.

EET216 Materials Science (2 units): Atomic and molecular structure; crystals; metallic states; defects in crystals; conductors, semiconductors and insulators. Alloy theory and its application to industrial alloys, steel in particular. Engineering properties and their control; hot and cold working; heat treatment. Creep, fatigue and fracture. Corrosion and corrosion control. Non-metallic materials — glass, rubber, concrete, plastics, wood and ceramics. Elastic and plastic deformation; defects in metals.

EET217 General Engineering Laboratory I (3 units): Practicals in all relevant courses taught in the semester.

EET218 Engineer-in-the-Society (1 unit): Philosophy of science; history of engineering and technology; safety in engineering and introduction to risk analysis; the role of engineers in nation building; invited lectures from professionals.

EET219 Basic Electrical Engineering I: Circuit elements, DC and AC circuits; basic circuit laws and theorems; resonance; power factor; three-phase circuits. Introduction to machines and machine design. Physics of devices — discharge devices and semiconductor devices: diodes (rectifier, varactor, Schottky, Zener) and transistors (BJT, FET); transistor characteristics, devices and circuits. Electrical and electrical power measurements.

sections.title: Course Descriptions — 200 Level Second Semester
sections.text:
MCE220 Fundamentals of Mechatronics (1 unit): Introduction to mechatronics — brief history, definition, elements and the disciplines involved. Characteristic advantages and disadvantages of mechatronic systems compared with non-mechatronic systems. Examples and areas of application. Measurement systems, control systems and microprocessor-based controllers. Sensors and transducers — performance terminology; sensors for displacement, position and proximity, velocity, motion, force, fluid pressure, liquid level, temperature and light; selection of sensors. Pneumatic and hydraulic systems — directional control valves and rotary actuators. Mechanical actuation systems — cams, gear trains, ratchet and pawl, belt and chain drives, bearings. Electrical actuation systems — mechanical switches, solid-state switches, solenoids, DC motors, AC motors and stepper motors. Fundamental concepts of creativity, innovation, development and entrepreneurship in developing mechatronics-based engineering solutions.

EET221 Engineering Mathematics II (3 units): Calculus — elementary differentiation and relevant theorems. Differential equations — exact equations; methods for second-order equations. Partial differential equations — simple cases and applications. Numerical analysis — linear and non-linear equations; finite difference operators. Introduction to linear programming.

EET222 Engineering Thermodynamics (2 units): Basic concepts, definitions and laws. The ideal gas, heat and work. The first law of thermodynamics and applications to open and closed systems. The steady-state flow equation (Bernoulli's equation) and applications. The second law of thermodynamics and heat cycles.

EET223 Engineering Drawing II (2 units): Continuation of Engineering Drawing I as mandatory drawing practice for engineers.

EET224 General Computer Programming (2 units): Program design using pseudo-code and flowcharts, with extensive engineering examples. Computer programming using C: symbols, keywords, identifiers, data types, operators, statements, flow of control, arrays, functions, file input and output. Graphics programming. Extensive examples and exercises solving engineering problems in C.

EET225 Workshop Practice (2 units): Types and organisation of engineering workshops — jobbing, batch and mass production. Engineering materials, their uses and properties. Safety in the workshop and general working principles. Bench work and fitting; hand tools and instruments. Carpentry — hand tools, materials, joints and timber processing. Blacksmithing — hand tools and working principles. Joints and fastenings — bolts, rivets, welding, brazing and soldering. Measurement and marking; standard measuring tools. Welding, brazing and soldering — principles, classification and power sources. Working principles of standard metal-cutting machine tools.

EET226 Information Technology in Engineering (2 units): Identification of PC parts and peripheral devices, their functions, applications and safe use; safety precautions and PC maintenance. Filing systems — directories, sub-directories and file paths. Word processing, the Internet (e-mail and WWW), spreadsheets, database management packages and report presentation software (such as PowerPoint), each with principles of operation, applications, demonstrations and hands-on exercises. A mini-project tests proficiency in the software packages. Impact of IT in engineering and emerging technologies.

EET227 General Engineering Laboratory II (3 units): Practicals in all relevant courses taught in the semester.

EET229 Basic Electrical Engineering II (2 units): Electricity power generation (hydro, thermal, gas, nuclear, MHD, geothermal). R-L-C AC circuits. Electrical machines: transformers (description, operation, losses, cooling methods, autotransformers, current transformers); DC motors and generators (characteristics, operation, equations, curves, types, applications).

ELE221 Basic Electronics (3 units): Number systems — binary, octal, decimal, hexadecimal and conversion. Logic gates — AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, Exclusive-OR (symbols, truth tables, logic expressions, realization using switches). Obtaining logic circuits from logic expressions and vice versa. Boolean algebra and simplification of logic expressions; Karnaugh maps; minterm and maxterm tables. Logic gates using transistors. Codes (BCD, ASCII, EBCDIC, Gray). Counters and registers. Applications — encoders, multiplexers, adders, RAM, ROM, PLAs. Introduction to microprocessors — basic microcomputer architecture, memory and applications.

SWEP — Students Work Experience Programme (2 units): Introduction to practices and skills in general engineering through instruction in the operation of hand and powered tools for wood and metal cutting and fabrication. Supervised hands-on experience in the safe use of tools and machines for selected tasks, over ten to twelve weeks during the long vacation.

sections.title: Course Descriptions — 300 Level First Semester
sections.text:
ELE311 Applied Mathematics for Electrical Engineering I (3 units, pre-requisite EET211): Linear algebra — matrix transformations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Fourier series and Fourier transforms; Laplace transforms; Gamma and Bessel functions; second-order differential equations; solutions of linear equations with constant coefficients; general, complementary and particular solutions; variable-coefficient linear equations. Probability and statistics — distribution and density functions, moments and moment-generating functions, standard distributions, correlation and regression. Vector calculus — gradient of a scalar point function, divergence and curl of a vector, second-order derivatives, with examples drawn from electrical engineering problems.

ELE312 Measurements and Instrumentation (3 units): Basic meter movements in DC and AC measurements — current, voltage, resistance, power and energy measurements; instrument transformers, current and voltage transformers. Bridge circuits — DC and AC bridges and their applications; LC meters. Digital measuring instruments — current, voltage, resistance, power and energy. Multimeters, oscilloscopes, waveform generators, pulse generators, waveform analyzers, counters, time-base circuits, analog and digital data acquisition systems, A/D and D/A converters, sample-and-hold circuits. Transducers and circuits — force, pressure, temperature, speed and flow measurements.

ELE313 Signals and Systems (2 units): Signals — classification (continuous/discrete-time, periodic/aperiodic) and properties (symmetry, even, odd, orthogonality). Processing systems — classification and properties (linearity, time-invariance, homogeneity). Signal sampling and the sampling theorem. Fourier transforms of aperiodic signals; frequency spectra; Rayleigh's theorem; frequency response. Time-domain models — discrete-time systems; unit-sample response; convolution (discrete and continuous); correlation. Application of Laplace and Hilbert transforms in system analysis. Z-transforms — determination methods, solution of difference equations, inverse Z-transform, frequency response and stability. Introduction to information theory and coding — entropy, Shannon's theorem and channel capacity; coding techniques with an illustration of Shannon-Fano coding.

ELE314 Circuit Theory (3 units): Review of Kirchhoff's laws; steady-state and transient analysis; Laplace transforms and their application to RL, RC and RLC circuits of one and two loops; initial and final value theorems; Fourier transformation in circuit analysis. Delta–wye transformation; superposition; reciprocity; Thevenin's and Norton's theorems; maximum power transfer. Foster–Cauer synthesis; one-port network synthesis; active filters. Approximation of non-linear characteristics of non-linear resistive circuits; harmonic analysis; sensitivity analysis. Use of computer simulation packages and an introduction to CAD.

ELE315 Analogue Electronic Circuits (3 units, pre-requisite ELE221): Diode models and circuits — rectifiers, clippers, clampers, switches, voltage multipliers and regulators. BJT circuits — configurations, biasing methods, single-stage small-signal amplifiers (equivalent circuits, voltage gain, current gain, power gain, input and output resistance, gain-frequency curve, bandwidth); multi-stage amplifiers and feedback. FET circuits — configuration, biasing, gain, input and output resistance, comparison with BJT. Power amplifiers (Class A, B, AB, C) operation and applications. Oscillator circuits — RC, LC, crystal, Wien bridge. Operational amplifiers — features and characteristics of ideal and non-ideal op-amps; op-amp circuits (summer, subtractor, integrator, differentiator, log and antilog amplifiers, voltage follower, oscillators, NIC).

ELE316 General Electrical Laboratory Practicals (3 units): Laboratory practicals covering topics in ELE311, ELE312, ELE313, ELE314, ELE315 and MCE311.

MCE311 Control Engineering I (2 units): Introduction; concepts of feedback control. Mathematical models of physical systems. Block diagrams and reduction techniques; block diagram algebra. Signal flow graphs and Mason's rule. Analysis and design in the s-plane. Steady-state and transient response to step and ramp inputs.

CPE311 Computer Programming and Languages (2 units): Introduction to software engineering fundamentals. Object-oriented programming. Number representations. Data structures and algorithms; abstraction, modules and objects; designing for efficiency. C++ object-oriented design paradigms and concepts — encapsulation and information hiding, separation of behaviour and implementation, classes, subclasses and inheritance, event-driven programming. Syntax and semantics of C++ — variables and types, expressions and assignments, simple input/output, conditional and iterative control structures, functions and parameter passing. Algorithms and flowcharts for C++ object-oriented problem solving — problem-solving strategies, the role of algorithms, implementation and debugging strategies, structured decomposition.

sections.title: Course Descriptions — 300 Level Second Semester
sections.text:
ELE321 Applied Mathematics for Electrical Engineering II (3 units, pre-requisite EET221): Complex numbers — analytic functions, functions of a complex variable, limits and continuity, Cauchy–Riemann equations, harmonic functions. Complex integration — contours and contour integrals, Cauchy's integral theorem and applications, residues, conformal mapping. Partial differential equations — basic concepts, vibrating strings, the one-dimensional wave equation, method of characteristics, separation of variables, line and multiple integrals. Introduction to numerical analysis with electrical engineering examples.

ELE322 Field Theory (3 units): Static fields — coordinate systems (Cartesian, cylindrical, spherical) and transformations between them. Gauss's, Ampere's and Faraday's laws; electrostatic fields due to charge distributions; magnetic fields in and around current-carrying conductors; Maxwell's equations. Dynamic fields — time-varying electric and magnetic fields; conduction and displacement currents; Maxwell's equations in the dynamic case; electromagnetic potential and the wave equation; the Poynting vector and electromagnetic energy; boundary conditions; wave propagation; skin effect; plane waves in unbounded dielectric media; fundamentals of transmission lines, waveguides and antennas.

ELE323 Principles of Electromechanical Conversion (2 units): Introduction to electromechanical energy conversion and rotating magnetic fields. Transformers — performance and parallel operation of single-phase transformers. DC machines — performance and methods of speed control. Induction machines — operation as a motor; performance of the single-phase induction motor. Synchronous machines — operation and performance as a generator; parallel operation of synchronous generators. Special machines — reluctance motors, hysteresis motors; faults on electrical machines.

ELE324 Digital Electronic Circuits (3 units, pre-requisite ELE221): Basic digital computer elements and logic circuits — practical representation and design principles of logic gates (DTL, DCTL, TTL) and memory elements; fan-in and fan-out. Common logic ICs. Combinational logic — multiplexers, comparators, half- and full-adders, design with NAND and NOR, multiple-output circuits, noise. Clock generation circuits — multivibrators, Schmitt triggers and time-base generators using discrete transistors and digital ICs; interfacing logic families. MSI circuits — scales of integration, design of MSI circuits, speed constraints and noise. Sequential digital circuits — Mealy–Moore circuits; flip-flops (SR, JK, T and D). Counters — binary, modulo-N, up/down; registers. Input/output circuits — synchronous circuits, clocking, clock rate and skew. Sequential finite state machines and algorithmic state machines. Programmable logic arrays (FPGA and others).

MCE321 Sensors and Actuators (3 units): Electrical actuators — review of electrical motors and their types; motor equations, drivers, and control of DC, induction, synchronous and stepper motors. Hydraulic actuators — pumps, hydraulic motors, valves and their types; power supplies; cylinders; accumulators; intensifiers; lifts; couplings; torque converters; hydraulic circuit design and analysis. Pneumatic actuators — compressors, fluid conditioners, pneumatic cylinders, valves and plugs; basic pneumatic circuit design and analysis; accumulator system analysis. Motion transducers — potentiometers, variable-inductance, permanent-magnet, variable-capacitance, piezoelectric and proximity transducers. Effort sensors — strain gauges, torque sensors and tactile sensors.

MCE322 Control Engineering II (2 units): Use of P+I, P+D, lag, lead and tacho compensators for improving overall response. Negative velocity and positive acceleration feedback. Error-rate damping. Stability analysis and Routh's stability criterion. Frequency response methods using polar, Bode and Nichols plots. Nyquist compensation. Design of systems with lead, lag and lead-lag compensators in the frequency domain. System identification from experimental data. Analog computing — basic computing elements, solutions of linear ODEs, simulation of simple transfer functions. DC bias design; analysis and design of single-stage and multi-stage amplifiers at low and high frequencies.

MCE323 Introduction to Robotics (3 units): Automation and robotics; robot classification and specifications. Direct kinematics — mathematical background, D-H representation, the arm equation, examples. Inverse kinematics — the inverse kinematics problem and its solution; tool configuration; examples of various robots. Introduction to manipulator dynamics — Lagrange's equation and the Lagrange-Euler dynamic model. Use of sensors and vision systems in robotic systems.

MCE324 Computer Software Engineering (2 units): Object-oriented software design, implementation and testing. Team software specification and management. Cross-platform tools and GUI development. Advanced software algorithms and architecture. Software engineering practice and methods.

MCE325 Mechatronics Systems Laboratory I (2 units): Laboratory practicals covering topics in ELE322, ELE323, ELE324, MCE321, MCE322, MCE323 and MCE324.

sections.title: Course Descriptions — 400 Level
sections.text:
ELE411 Introduction to Research Methods and Engineering Communications (2 units): Elements of research — concept and need, types of research, steps in conducting research, the research problem and its definition, methods of knowing and methodology. Elements of technical communication — professional use of English and principles of technical report writing (term papers, long essays, project reports, theses and dissertations). Oral presentation of technical ideas — presentation guides and the use of presentation software (PowerPoint, Harvard Graphics, LaTeX).

MCE411 Fluid Power Systems II (2 units, pre-requisite EET214): Physical properties of fluids; fluid statics; fluid motion; conservation laws for mass, momentum and energy. Fluid friction and the energy equation in viscous flow. Laminar flow — steady flow in pipes and between parallel plates. Viscous flow theory and applications. Mechanical power systems and operations. Drive requirements for mechanical equipment. Thermal and hydraulic power systems. Introduction to heat exchangers.

MCE412 Computer Aided Design and Manufacturing (2 units): The design process and design concepts; sensors and actuators; computer vision; digital data acquisition and processing. Analysis and design of individual machine components — shafts, gears, chain linkages, bearings, keys, keyways, belts and clutches; component assemblies and machine systems. In-depth study of advanced technologies adopted by leading design and manufacturing industries worldwide, exploring rapid product development and technologies aimed at reducing product development lead-time within a Design for Manufacture context.

MCE413 Mechatronics Systems Design (3 units): Introduction to the mechatronics system design approach, tools, simulations, mechanical systems and mechanisms. Key components in mechatronic systems; design approach and philosophy. Introduction to microcomputers; hardwired versus programmed logic; microcomputer applications. Elements of microcomputer architecture — bus, microprocessor, memory, input/output and peripherals; single-chip and multi-chip microcomputers. Internal architecture — the three-bus concept and microprocessor operation. Microprocessor instruction sets — instruction formats, addressing modes and instruction execution; comparison of available microprocessors. Machine language, assembly language and high-level language programming. Synthesis of combinational logic circuits with ROMs and PLAs. Classical sequential circuit design and the algorithmic state machine (ASM) chart method. Realization of sequential circuits using MSI and LSI; register transfer languages.

MCE414 MEMS and VLSI (2 units): Basic microelectronic devices and a brief review of the physics involved. Fabrication technology of microelectronic devices. IC fabrication technology (CMOS). Silicon crystal growth and epitaxy. Ion implantation, etching, chemical vapour deposition and photolithography. Silicon bulk and surface micromachining technology for microsystems and MEMS.

MCE415 Digital Image Processing Systems and Application (2–3 units): Introduction to digital image processing and its fundamentals; relationships between pixels. Intensity transformations and spatial filtering — histogram processing, smoothing and sharpening filters, combined spatial enhancement, fuzzy techniques. Filtering in the frequency domain — image smoothing, sharpening and selective filtering. Image restoration and reconstruction — the image degradation/restoration model. Colour image processing — colour transformations, smoothing and sharpening, segmentation based on colour, noise in colour images. Wavelets and multiresolution processing. Image compression. Morphological image processing — erosion and dilation, opening and closing. Image segmentation — point, line and edge detection, thresholding and region-based segmentation.

MCE416 Mechatronics System Laboratory II (2 units): Laboratory practicals covering topics in MCE411, MCE412, MCE413, MCE414 and MCE415.

MCE400 Mechatronics Capstone Project (2 units): Identifying problem requirements. Generating and evaluating design concepts; design and fabrication. Design of control software. Testing and debugging of systems. Documentation of design and results.

sections.title: Course Descriptions — 500 Level First Semester
sections.text:
ELE511 Management and Law for Electrical Engineers (2 units): Principles of management and organizational behaviour. Needs theory and motivation. Introduction to industrial relations and collective bargaining. Industrial law; legislation on wages, trademarks and patents; law of contract and sale of goods; liability for industrial injuries. Case studies and reviews relating to electrical engineering.

ELE512 Digital Signal Processing (2 units): Digital Fourier transform; Fast Fourier transform; the approximation problem in network theory; synthesis of low-pass filters; special transforms and their application in the synthesis of high-pass and band-pass filters; digital filtering transfer function analysis; one-dimensional recursive and non-recursive filters; computer techniques in filter analysis; realization of filters in hardware and software; basic image processing concepts.

EEE514 Power Electronics and Drives (2 units): Power electronics — switching characteristics of diodes, transistors and thyristors; analysis of diode circuits with reactive loads; transistor power control circuits; AC/DC converters; characteristics of switching transformers; power semiconductor protection; examples of power electronic circuits; solar devices. Drives — fundamentals of electric drives; speed control; control sensors for displacement, velocity, power factor and reactive power; motor power rating; selection and load diagrams; automatic electric drives; linear motors.

CPE510 Artificial Intelligence and Applications (2 units): Introduction to artificial intelligence and its engineering applications — problem-solving techniques, knowledge acquisition, knowledge representation, production systems, expert systems, AI languages, neural networks and machine learning. Design projects are required.

MCE511 Robotics and Automation (2 units, pre-requisite MCE323): Introduction to automation — economics of automation, flow lines, mathematical models, storage buffers, partial automation, balancing, group technology and flexible manufacturing. Programmable Logic Controllers — introduction and advantages, ladder logic diagrams, switching logic, PLC components and operating cycle, latches, design cases (deadman switches, conveyors, accept/reject sorting), addressing, PLC connection and operation, numbering, event-based logic, sequential logic design, advanced ladder logic functions. PLC programming — structured text, instruction list and function block programming; continuous control; PLC data communication; Human-Machine Interfaces (HMI); selecting a PLC. CNC machines — general information, operation, control panel, tool functions, tool wear offsets, feed and spindle functions, programming of CNC in absolute and incremental systems, program creation, preparatory functions and NC programming. Computer-assisted part programming, automatically programmed tools (the APT programming system), the CAD/CAM approach to part programming and CAD/CAM applications (turning, surface milling, machining of curved surfaces).

MCE512 Vibration (2 units): Mechanical systems with one and several degrees of freedom; free, forced and damped vibrations. Vibration problem solution by modal analysis. Continuous systems, including exact and finite-element methods. Approximate methods of solution; computer solutions. Vibration isolation and absorption. Machine balancing.

MCE513 Digital Systems and PLC (2 units): Digital representation of information and binary arithmetic. Positional number systems; binary coding of alphanumeric characters; error detecting and correcting codes (parity bits, Hamming codes). Boolean algebra, switching functions, truth tables and Karnaugh maps; canonical forms; don't-cares; minimization of multiple-output switching functions; combinational circuit design — encoders, decoders, multiplexers, serial and parallel half- and full-adders. Hazards in combinational circuits. Feedback, state and delay in logic circuits; synchronous sequential circuits; state transition equations, diagrams and tables; clocked flip-flops (RS, JK, T); edge-triggered and master-slave flip-flops.

MCE531 Machine Vision (elective, 2 units): Advanced techniques and algorithms for real-time computer vision and image processing design. Machine vision, image geometry, sampling and quantization. Image representation — digitization, digital image properties, colour images and cameras. Image formation physics — radiometric measurement, capture and optics, lens aberration and distortion, surface reflectance. Data structures for image analysis — matrices, chains, topological and relational structures, pyramids, quad-trees. Image pre-processing — pixel brightness and geometric transformations, local pre-processing, restoration. Segmentation — thresholding, edge-based and region-based segmentation, matching, texture. Object recognition — region identification, contour- and region-based shape representation, shape classes, knowledge representation, graph matching and optimization techniques. Image understanding — control strategies, RANSAC, point distribution models, scene labelling, semantic segmentation. 3D vision — projective geometry, scene reconstruction from multiple views, stereo vision, trifocal sensors. Dynamic vision — change detection, segmentation using motion, motion correspondence, image flow, tracking and shape from motion.

MCE532 Modern Control (elective, 2 units, pre-requisite MCE311): Review of classical control systems — performance and stability, root locus analysis and design, frequency response analysis and design. Advanced classical control — PID tuning using the Ziegler–Nichols rule, modified PID controllers, two-DOF control, robust PID control and robust internal model control. Full state feedback design — controllability and observability, pole placement, Ackermann's formula and servo system design. State observers — full-order and reduced-order observers with pole-placement design. Optimal control — types of optimal control problems, selection of performance indices, the linear quadratic regulator. Introduction to nonlinear control — common nonlinearities in mechatronic systems, describing functions, Lyapunov stability and feedback linearization.

EEE518 Energy Studies (elective, 2 units): Global energy assessment. Primary and secondary energy sources. Renewable and non-renewable energy resources. Energy needs of the country. Energy conversion techniques. Energy conservation, energy management and auditing.

CPE519 Internet of Things (elective, 2 units): Definition and significance of the Internet of Things; architecture, operation, embedded system applications and interfacing with IoT; business benefits and opportunities of IoT solutions; the relationship between IoT, cloud computing and big data; how IoT differs from traditional data collection systems and networks. IoT sensor utilization and data collection; IoT data collection and analysis in the cloud; implementing a multi-node IoT solution; designing an IoT solution.

sections.title: Course Descriptions — 500 Level Second Semester
sections.text:
ELE521 Reliability Methods in Electrical Engineering and Technology: Basic reliability concepts — definition and need for reliability, reliability programme plans, block diagrams, series, parallel, series-parallel and redundant systems. Reliability distributions — failure-time distributions, derivation of the bathtub hazard function, the exponential model. Reliability in design — fault-tree analysis, FMEA, FMECA, parts count and parts stress analysis. Reliability assessment at the production phase — Weibull analysis, the Duane model and reliability growth. Operating reliability assessment — techniques, degraded reliability tests, maintainability and availability, organizing for reliability, economics of reliability. Applications — reliability specification and metrics for computer hardware, electronic/communication and electrical power systems.

MCE521 Microcontrollers and Embedded Systems (2 units, pre-requisite MCE413): Embedded systems and microcontroller programming; microprocessors and microcontrollers, PLC and PIC microcontrollers; programming a PIC. Sensors — performance, signal conditioning and selection. Data acquisition — D/A and A/D conversion and selection. Communication systems — digital communication, protocols, communication interfaces, USB and remote communication (infrared, RFID). Introduction to the PIC18Fxx2; assembly language programming — 8-bit signed and unsigned operations, comparisons, subroutines, stacks, pointers and table reads. C language programming — compilation, PIC18 hardware, power consumption, watchdog timers, sleep mode, datasheets, state machine programming, LED/switch I/O and LCD module interfacing. Inputs and outputs — parallel port operation, I/O channels, synchronous and asynchronous serial I/O, I2C and serial EEPROM. Interrupts and timers — PWM, DC motors and servos, waveform generation, interrupt-driven I/O. Embedded systems in mechatronics applications — audio record/playback systems, home monitoring systems, digital thermometers and autonomous robots.

MCE522 Process Control and Automation (2 units, pre-requisite MCE322): Overview of industrial automation. Process parameters — temperature, pressure, level, flow and flowrate and their metering systems; calibration techniques. Introduction to industrial automation, production and support equipment, control and feedback devices, design considerations and cost justification. Industrial sensors, actuators and vision systems — types, selection criteria and applications. Industrial process control systems — on-off control. Programmable Logic Controllers — fundamentals of PLC programming, components of PLC systems, applications, ladder and other PLC languages, brands of PLC. Relays — coil and contact circuits. Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) — fundamentals, architecture, generations and types; simple SCADA design. Distributed Control Systems (DCS) — fundamentals, architecture, generations and types; simple DCS design; application of DCS in industrial process control using Honeywell or ABB DCS. PID control systems — integration of PID into PLC-operated systems and PID tuning; industrial process reaction delays; components of industrial flow control processes. P&ID instrumentation — fundamentals of P&ID diagrams, safety instrumented systems and configuration, P&ID documentation schemes, lines, valves and tags.

MCE523 Systems Modelling and Simulation (2 units): Basic concepts of physical modelling and system identification; review of dynamic models of mechanical, electrical and electromechanical systems. Physical modelling using bond graphs — effort and flow, junctions, transformers and gyrators, causality, state equations from bond graphs. Introduction to system identification — basic concepts, review of signals and systems and stochastic processes, basic steps in the identification process. Design of experiments — information and data collection; input signal design and implementation; the use and design of random and deterministic input signals (pulse, step, random binary sequence, pseudo-random binary sequence). Model validation — residual analysis, whiteness of the residue, autocorrelation tests, the Akaike information criterion, final prediction error and independent data testing.

MCE599 Final Year Project (6 units): Each student is expected to solve a research problem using principles, concepts and methodologies in any area of Mechatronics Engineering, under the supervision of academic staff in the department.

MCE541 Intelligent Control Systems (elective, 2 units, pre-requisite MCE322): Review of the fundamentals of process control — basis, terminologies, design and implementation. Modelling of process control systems; design and implementation of feedback, feedforward and inferential control strategies in single and multi-loop systems. Review of PID control types and tuning techniques. Introduction to multivariable control and predictive control. Use of MATLAB/Simulink for simulating process-control-based systems. Review of intelligent systems — concepts, fuzzy logic and artificial neural networks. Case studies of controller development using intelligent tuning algorithms.

MCE542 Digital Signal Processor-Based Systems (elective, 2 units): Discrete-time signals and systems — LTI systems, frequency-domain representation, Fourier-transform representation of sequences, discrete-time random signals, the Z-transform. Sampling of continuous-time signals — periodic sampling and reconstruction of band-limited signals. Structures for discrete-time systems — block diagrams and signal flow graphs, IIR structures, transposed forms, FIR structures. Introduction to DSP controllers — the TMS320LF2407 and its peripherals, physical memory and software tools. The C2xx DSP CPU and instruction set — core components, mapping external devices, system configuration registers, memory addressing modes and assembly programming. General-purpose I/O — pin multiplexing, GP registers and ports. Interrupts on the TMS320LF2407 — interrupt hierarchy and control registers. The analog-to-digital converter — operation, sequencer configuration, operating modes and triggering sources. The event managers — interrupts, flag registers, general-purpose timers, PWM output, compare operation, dead-band generation, capture units and quadrature encoded pulses (QEP).

MCE543 Autonomous and Mobile Robotics Systems (elective, 2 units, pre-requisite MCE323): Review of the fundamentals of robotic systems. Mobile robots and autonomous systems. Locomotion — key issues, wheeled and legged mobile robots. Mobile robot kinematics — kinematic models and constraints, maneuverability, workspace and motion control. Perception — sensors for mobile robots, sensor classification, characterization and performance measures; uncertainty and statistical representation; error propagation. Mobile robot localization — noise and aliasing, belief and map representation, probabilistic map-based localization, landmark-based navigation, globally unique localization, positioning beacon systems, route-based localization and autonomous map building. Planning and navigation — competencies for navigation, path planning, obstacle avoidance, navigation architectures, control localization, decomposition techniques and case studies.

sections.title: Structure of Programme Implementation
sections.text:
Lectures are delivered through a combination of formal lectures, tutorials, practical sessions, laboratory work, seminars and the incorporation of information and communication technology (computing facilities). Students are evaluated through: (a) Continuous Assessment, made up of assignments (written or oral) and formal tests, forming 40% of the evaluation; and (b) a formal Examination making up 60% of the evaluation.

100 Level examinations are multiple-choice question types, while 200 to 500 Level examinations are short-essay or long-essay types.

sections.title: Areas of Practical Experience (SWEP and SIWES)
sections.text:
Industrial training is an integral part of the five-year degree programme. It is made up of ten (10) weeks of the Students Work Experience Programme (SWEP) at the end of 200 Level, the Student Industrial Work Experience Scheme I (SIWES I) at the end of 300 Level, and twenty-four (24) weeks of the Student Industrial Work Experience Scheme II (SIWES II) during the second semester of 400 Level, i.e. after the first-semester 400 Level examinations.

An academically weak student may be advised to defer SIWES II until he or she clears all carry-over (failed) courses. Such a student must satisfy the SIWES II requirements before proceeding to 500 Level. Note: students on SIWES cannot concurrently register for or take any course during the semester while undertaking SIWES II.

sections.title: Grading System
sections.text: The Federal University of Technology, Minna and the Department of Mechatronics Engineering operate a 5.0 grading system. The grades, grade points and score ranges are: A — 5.0 grade points, 70–100%, Excellent; B — 4.0 grade points, 60–69%, Very Good; C — 3.0 grade points, 50–59%, Good; D — 2.0 grade points, 45–49%, Satisfactory; E — 1.0 grade point, 40–44%, Fair; F — 0.0 grade points, below 40%, Failure.

sections.title: Computation of Results (GPA and CGPA)
sections.text: The University operates a 5.0 grade point system, and all semesters cumulatively contribute to the class of degree a student graduates with. Key terms: (1) Semesterial Courses Taken (SCT) — the total number of course units carried in a particular semester; for instance, a student taking 6 courses of 3 units each has SCT = 18. (2) Total Courses Taken (TCT) — the summation of course units taken over all semesters to date. (3) Semesterial Grade Point (SGP) — the sum of the products of course units and grade rating for each course in the semester; for example, with six 3-unit courses graded A, B, C, D, E and F, SGP = 3×5 + 3×4 + 3×3 + 3×2 + 3×1 + 3×0 = 45. (4) Cumulative Grade Point (CGP) — the summation of SGP over all semesters from the first semester. (5) Grade Point Average (GPA) — the SGP divided by the SCT; from the example, GPA = 45/18 = 2.5. (6) Cumulative Grade Point Average (CGPA) — not the summation of GPAs, but the summation of SGP for all semesters to date (CGP) divided by the summation of SCT (TCT): CGPA = CGP/TCT.

sections.title: Class of Degree
sections.text:
Classes of degree by CGPA: First Class — 4.5 to 5.0; Second Class Upper — 3.5 to 4.49; Second Class Lower — 2.40 to 3.49; Third Class — 1.50 to 2.39; Pass — 1.00 to 1.49; Fail — 0.00 to 0.99.

Terminologies: the unit of a course is equivalent to the weekly lecture duration for that course. A core course is one which must be registered for and passed by a student to get the degree and is counted towards the classification of the degree. An elective course is either compulsory or optional: a compulsory elective is counted towards the classification of the degree, while an optional elective may be taken by the student and may not be counted towards the classification of the degree.

sections.title: Mode of Assessment
sections.text: The Mechatronics Engineering Department has three modes of assessing students for any given course: (1) practical assessment; (2) oral assessment; and (3) written or electronic examination. The particular mode employed in a course is dictated by the course type and is the prerogative of the lecturer and the department.

sections.title: Classification Based on Student Performance
sections.text: Vice Chancellor's List (VCL): a student with a CGPA of 4.5 and above at the end of the session is placed on the VCL for as long as the CGPA does not go below 4.5, and is eligible for a school fee waiver while the status is maintained. Dean's List (DL): a student with a CGPA of 4.0 and above is placed on the DL and receives a letter from the Dean's office. In Good Standing (IGS): a student without any carry-over or outstanding courses. Deficiency (DEF): any course failed must be repeated until passed; a student may repeat only courses in which an F was obtained, and the grades earned for a repeated course are all recorded and used in computing the CGPA. Semester Probation (P): a student with a CGPA below 1.50 at the end of a semester is placed on semester probation. Sessional Probation (SP1): any student with a CGPA below 1.5 at the end of 100 Level will be withdrawn from the University. Withdrawal (SP2): a student already on sessional probation who fails to improve by the end of the second session will be withdrawn from the university.

sections.title: Regulations on Course Registration
sections.text: Registration of courses is done online. All registration must be concluded before the matriculation of new students. Failure to register on time attracts a penalty fee as stipulated by the University Senate. Failure to register in time to meet 70% attendance at lectures for the semester may result in the student being made to repeat the semester or withdraw from the university, as the case may be. A student cannot re-register for a course already passed.

sections.title: Regulations on Admission Deferment
sections.text: A student is allowed to defer their academic programme, on a semester basis, on any of the following grounds: health or medical reasons; financial reasons; academic reasons; or any other reason deemed acceptable by the Department, the School and the Senate of the University. A student is expected to register first before applying for deferment. Note that a deferred semester or session counts towards the student's residency period.

sections.title: Condonation, Absenteeism and Residency Duration
sections.text:
Condonation applies to a student who has officially informed the University earlier of problems based on health or medical grounds, academic grounds, or any other reason deemed acceptable by the Department. A condoned semester or session does not count towards the student's residency period.

Residency: a student is allowed by the University laws to spend 150% of the minimum duration of their entry mode; on exceeding this, they are required to vacate the University. Residency durations by mode of admission are: UTME (100 Level) — seven and a half academic sessions; Direct Entry at 200 Level — six academic sessions; Direct Entry at 300 Level — four and a half academic sessions.

Absenteeism: any student who absents himself or herself from the University for two consecutive academic semesters is deemed to have forfeited those semesters, and beyond that the student is deemed to have voluntarily withdrawn from the programme.

sections.title: Requirements to Proceed from 100 Level to 200 Level
sections.text: To proceed to 200 Level from 100 Level, the following minimum requirements must be met at the end of 100 Level: (1) satisfy the 8:8:6 requirement as stipulated by the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN), meaning a student must have passed a minimum of 8 credit units of Mathematics, 8 credit units of Physics and 6 credit units of Chemistry; (2) obtain a Cumulative Grade Point Average (CGPA) of not less than 2.0. Any student who fails to meet these two conditions is to be withdrawn from the School of Engineering and Engineering Technology.

sections.title: Examination Regulations
sections.text: It is mandatory for a student to have 75% attendance to qualify to sit for the examination in any course taken. The setting, conduct, evaluation schemes, internal and external moderation schemes for degree examinations, and the issuance of results follow the Approved Senate Regulations Governing the Conduct of Examinations and the General Academic Regulations for degree courses.

sections.title: General Academic Regulations for Degree Courses
sections.text:
Definition of units: the unit of a course is the semester unit — one semester unit is when a class meets one hour every week for the semester, or three to four hours every week in the laboratory for the semester, or the equivalent in workshop or fieldwork time. The size of a course shall normally be a maximum of three units and last one semester, except for projects and design courses, which may carry more than three units and last more than one semester.

Course types: (i) a core course must be registered for and passed to earn the degree and counts towards its classification; (ii) an elective course is either compulsory or optional — all elective courses taken are used in the final computation for the degree classification; (iii) a University-required course is a compulsory course prescribed by the university which must be passed before graduation and also counts towards the classification; (iv) an audited course is one the student attends without writing its examination; (v) a pre-requisite course must be passed before proceeding to the higher course; (vi) a co-requisite course may be taken in parallel with the course for which it is specified.

Duration of the semester: during each semester, 15 weeks (exclusive of vacations and mid-semester breaks) are normally reserved for teaching, and two weeks for examinations.

sections.title: Regulations on Continuous Assessment
sections.text:
Assessment of a student's achievement shall be continuous, and the student shall be periodically informed of his or her standing in the course. The final examination for each course is normally at the end of the semester in which the course is offered. The course grade is made up of the student's continuous assessment score and the end-of-course examination; continuous assessment carries a maximum of 40%.

As part of the policy of maintaining high academic standards, the Department stipulates conditions requiring students to attain certain grades in specific subjects before being absorbed into the department from 100 Level: 10 credit units of Mathematics, 8 credit units of Physics and 8 credit units of Chemistry. In addition, a student must have a CGPA of 2.0 and above to remain in good academic standing. Students with the best sessional CGPA greater than 4.5 at each level of study are usually recommended for the University Scholarship.

sections.title: Professional Examinations and Registration
sections.text: Graduates of Mechatronics Engineering are qualified to sit for the qualifying examinations and become registered members of the following professional bodies: (i) Member, Nigerian Society of Engineers (MNSE); and (ii) Registered Engineer with the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN).

sections.title: Conduct of Laboratory Experiments
sections.text:
Laboratory experiments are conducted at various levels. Most 100 and 200 Level courses are common to all engineering students, so experiments at these two levels are conducted by the departments that service the courses. Core Mechatronics engineering experiments and project work commence during the second semester of 300 Level, when students have acquired relevant engineering practical skills in the other areas of engineering: mechanical, computer, communication and electrical.

The department runs Mechatronics Laboratory Practices. Students' laboratory reports and the standard Laboratory Manual for relevant experiments in Mechatronics Systems Design are available at the Mechatronics System Laboratory. Other laboratory practices cognate to Mechatronics Engineering are serviced by other laboratories in the University — for example, Data Communication and Networks I and II at the Telecommunication Engineering Laboratories; Logic Circuits and Digital Electronics at the Digital Electronics Laboratory and Central Teaching Laboratory; Control Engineering at the Control Engineering Laboratory; and Introduction to Mechatronics at the Mechatronics and Autotronics Laboratory in the Electrical and Electronics Engineering Department. Practical and SIWES logbooks are made available to students upon attaining the appropriate levels.

sections.title: Examination Policy and Result Approval
sections.text: Examinations are set by the individual lecturers for the courses taught. After moderation of the questions at a meeting of departmental academic staff, the questions are administered for each semester examination by the School examination office. Final-year questions are moderated by an external examiner. Results of examinations are considered and approved at a meeting of the academic staff of the department, then forwarded for consideration and approval by both the School Academic Board and the University Senate before being released to students. Students must also conduct themselves properly in examination halls, in line with the University's rules and regulations on examination misconduct.

sections.title: Examination Misconduct — Offences Before the Examination
sections.text: Offences before the examination and their penalties: writing before the official commencement of the examination — delay for 10 minutes during the course of the examination; forging any document relevant to the examination (e.g. ID card or school fee payment receipt) — expulsion; refusing to be identified and/or searched at the entrance of the examination hall — exclusion from that particular paper; staff harassment or intimidation for leakage of examination questions — expulsion; smuggling blank answer booklets or continuation sheets in or out of the examination hall — expulsion; involvement in an examination leakage — expulsion.

sections.title: Examination Misconduct — Offences During the Examination
sections.text: Offences during the examination and their penalties: writing beyond the official termination of the examination — deduction of 5 marks on the spot by the chief invigilator; talking to another student during the examination — deduction of 5 marks; writing on the question paper — deduction of 10 marks; being caught with extraneous material not relevant to the examination — expulsion; using foreign material relevant to the examination or course inside the hall — expulsion; bringing relevant materials into the hall even if not caught using them — expulsion; violating the sitting arrangement (e.g. changing position without permission) — cancellation of the paper; bringing an already-written answer script or continuation sheet into the hall — expulsion; aiding and abetting examination misconduct (e.g. transferring materials or deliberately exposing an answer booklet for others to copy) — suspension for two semesters; giving false information during the examination or investigation — suspension for two semesters; being found guilty of examination misconduct a second time after a previous conviction — expulsion; assaulting or fighting an invigilator or any officer of the University — expulsion; impersonation (both the impersonator and the collaborator) — expulsion; failing to submit the answer script at the end of the examination — suspension for two semesters and cancellation of the paper; failure to sign out at the end of the examination — cancellation of the paper; refusing to surrender incriminating evidence, or chewing or destroying materials — expulsion; refusing to write a statement in respect of alleged examination misconduct — expulsion; transferring or receiving any materials to or from another student during the examination without permission — expulsion; taking a GSM handset (mobile phone) into the examination hall — expulsion; exchanging calculators in the examination hall without permission — expulsion; exchanging answer booklets in the examination hall — expulsion; being in possession of dangerous weapons in and around the examination hall — expulsion; writing on any part of the body or clothes, whether relevant or not — expulsion; being caught with relevant writing or material at the back of a calculator, including placing material inside the maths set — expulsion.

sections.title: Examination Misconduct — Offences After the Examination
sections.text: Offences after the examination and their penalties: refusal to give evidence before the Examination Misconduct Committee as a confirmed witness — expulsion; refusal to appear before the Examination Misconduct Committee after being invited on three occasions, where the invitations were confirmed to have been delivered to the student through an authentic channel — expulsion.

sections.title: Mandatory Engineering Drawing Practice
sections.text: The mandatory practice of engineering drawing in the training of engineers is observed in Engineering Drawing I and Engineering Drawing II at the 200 Level.

sections.title: Mandatory Industrial Training Programme
sections.text:
One year of industrial training is an integral part of the five-year degree programme. It is made up of ten (10) weeks of the Students Work Experience Programme (SWEP) at the end of 200 Level, twelve (12) weeks of the Student Industrial Work Experience Scheme I (SIWES I) at the end of 300 Level, and twenty-four (24) weeks of the Student Industrial Work Experience Scheme II (SIWES II) during the second semester of 400 Level.

The schedule of mandatory school and industry work experience is: SWEP — 6 weeks, in the School, at the end of 200 Level; SIWES I — 12 weeks, in industry, at the end of 300 Level; SIWES II — 24 weeks, in industry, at the end of the first semester of 400 Level.

An academically weak student may defer SIWES II until all carry-over courses are cleared, and must satisfy the SIWES requirements before being allowed to proceed to 500 Level. Students on SIWES cannot register for or take any course during that semester.

sections.title: Regulation on the Award of the Degree
sections.text:
The nomenclature of the degree awarded by the Department is Bachelor of Engineering — B.Eng. (Mechatronics Engineering). To be eligible for the award, a student must have: (a) passed all core (compulsory) courses, all University and School required courses, and the electives recommended for specialization; and (b) successfully completed all class work, industrial attachments, seminars and projects.

To graduate, a student must be found worthy in character throughout the period of studentship and must accumulate the total units prescribed by the School from core, elective and General Studies courses, SWEP/SIWES and the project. A student must be in good standing in order to go for Industrial Attachment.

sections.title: Intra- and Inter-University Transfers
sections.text:
All candidates seeking transfer, whether intra- or inter-university, must have spent a minimum of one academic session in the programme of first admission, with the full sessional result attached to the application for transfer.
